figures.title: The Antinutrient Family Tree
figures.subtitle: Six natural compounds, grouped by what they block.

segments.name: Antinutrients
segments.text: This lesson is about antinutrients: compounds that plants make naturally which reduce how well you absorb or use a nutrient. There are six main ones, and this tree sorts them by what they block.

segments.name: Three Groups
segments.text: Phytate, oxalate and tannins bind minerals like iron, zinc and calcium. Lectins and trypsin inhibitors get in the way of protein digestion. And goitrogens get in the way of iodine.
segments.cue: The second and third rows, left to right

segments.name: Foods and Fixes
segments.text: Under each one are the foods it's highest in, and the kitchen fix: soaking, sprouting, fermenting, boiling or simply cooking. Each box links to its figure.

segments.name: Why Plants Make Them
segments.text: Plants don't make these to harm us. They store phosphorus, or deter insects and animals. They just happen to interfere with a nutrient when we eat them.

segments.name: Not on the Label
segments.text: Traditional ways of preparing grains and beans grew up partly because they reduce antinutrients. And because they occur naturally, you'll never see them on a label.

figures.title: What Makes an Antinutrient
figures.subtitle: The minerals they grip, and three ways to block a nutrient.

segments.name: The Minerals
segments.text: Let's start with what gets blocked. Zinc, iron and calcium travel through your gut as small positive ions, drawn here at the same scale as every molecule on the page.

segments.name: Gripping Ions
segments.text: Many antinutrients carry negative oxygen groups that grip those ions. The clump is too big or too insoluble to cross the gut wall, so the mineral simply passes through.

segments.name: Three Ways
segments.text: There are three ways to block a nutrient: grip minerals, block a digestive enzyme or stick to the gut wall, or get in the way of the thyroid.

segments.name: Dose and Context
segments.text: For most people eating a varied diet, antinutrients matter little. They matter more when one staple food supplies most of the calories, when mineral intake is already low, or in vegan diets that rely on grains and beans for iron and zinc.

segments.name: Often Useful Too
segments.text: And many of the same compounds have benefits. Phytate and tannins are antioxidants, and the foods richest in them are linked to better health. We'll meet that side in the Bioactives lesson.

figures.title: Phytate
figures.subtitle: Inositol with six phosphates: the seed’s phosphorus store.

segments.name: Two Building Blocks
segments.text: Phytate is built from two parts. Inositol is a ring of six carbons with an OH on every one, a close cousin of glucose. And phosphate is the same group that's in DNA and ATP.

segments.name: Six Phosphates
segments.text: Put a phosphate on all six carbons and you get phytic acid. In the gut its phosphates lose hydrogens and carry negative charges, and those grip zinc, iron and calcium.

segments.name: The Seed’s Store
segments.text: Phytate is how seeds store phosphorus for the sprouting plant. Humans make very little phytase, the enzyme that cuts it apart, so most phytate passes through, taking bound minerals with it. It's the main thing in food that lowers zinc absorption.

segments.name: Too Much
segments.text: Diets high in phytate and low in meat can lead to zinc and iron deficiency, especially where one unrefined grain or bean is the main food. But phytate is also an antioxidant, and whole-grain diets are linked to lower disease risk.

segments.name: Found In
segments.text: It's in the bran of whole grains, beans, lentils, soy, nuts and seeds. Refined white flour has much less, because the bran is removed.

figures.title: Oxalate
figures.subtitle: A tiny acid that locks up calcium.

segments.name: Oxalic Acid
segments.text: Oxalic acid is the smallest acid with two acid groups: just two carbons and four oxygens.

segments.name: Grabbing Calcium
segments.text: In food it loses both hydrogens, leaving oxalate with two negative charges, and those clamp onto calcium. Calcium oxalate barely dissolves, so it forms crystals.

segments.name: Spinach Calcium
segments.text: Oxalate binds calcium in the gut, so the calcium in spinach is absorbed only about a fifth as well as the calcium in milk.

segments.name: Kidney Stones
segments.text: Absorbed oxalate leaves in urine, where it can join calcium to form kidney stones; most kidney stones are calcium oxalate. People who form stones are often told to limit high-oxalate foods, drink plenty of fluid, and eat calcium with those foods, which binds the oxalate in the gut.

segments.name: Found In
segments.text: Spinach, rhubarb, Swiss chard, beet greens, almonds, cashews, cocoa and sweet potatoes are high in oxalate. Rhubarb leaves are poisonous, so eat only the stalks.

figures.title: Tannins
figures.subtitle: Polyphenols that grip iron and proteins.

segments.name: Gallic Acid
segments.text: Tannins are big polyphenols built from two kinds of building block. Gallic acid has three OH groups side by side on a ring, a strong grip for iron. Many gallic acids joined to a sugar make a hydrolyzable tannin.

segments.name: Catechin
segments.text: Catechin has two neighboring OH groups on its ring, the same kind of grip. Chains of catechin-type units make condensed tannins.

segments.name: Astringency
segments.text: Tannins bind proteins, and that's the dry, puckering feel of strong tea, red wine and unripe fruit.

segments.name: Iron
segments.text: They also bind nonheme iron. Tea with a meal can cut the iron you absorb from it by more than half, and coffee does something similar. Heme iron from meat is much less affected. So if your iron is low, drink tea and coffee between meals.

segments.name: Found In
segments.text: Tea, red wine, coffee, cocoa, pomegranate, persimmons, grape skins, sorghum and colored beans are rich in tannins and related polyphenols.

figures.title: Lectins and Trypsin Inhibitors
figures.subtitle: Proteins that stick to the gut or plug an enzyme.

segments.name: Lectins
segments.text: Lectins are proteins that bind specific sugars. The cells lining your gut are coated with sugar chains, and some lectins clamp onto them. They resist digestion and can damage the lining.

segments.name: Raw Kidney Beans
segments.text: The best-known lectin is in red kidney beans. Raw or undercooked, as few as four or five beans can cause severe vomiting and diarrhea within hours. Beans warmed but not boiled, as in some slow cookers, can be worse than raw.

segments.name: Boil Them
segments.text: The fix is simple: soak dried beans, pour off the water, and boil them hard. Boiling destroys almost all lectin activity, and canned beans are already cooked.

segments.name: Trypsin Inhibitors
segments.text: Trypsin is an enzyme from your pancreas that cuts proteins apart. A trypsin inhibitor is a small protein that fits tightly into trypsin's cutting site, like a plug, so less protein gets digested. Heat unfolds the inhibitor so it no longer fits.

segments.name: Raw Soybeans
segments.text: Animals fed raw soybeans grow poorly. In people it's rarely a problem, because soy is almost always cooked, toasted or fermented. Raw egg white and raw potatoes have inhibitors too.

figures.title: Goitrogens
figures.subtitle: Compounds that get in the way of iodine.

segments.name: Iodide
segments.text: Your thyroid pulls iodide from the blood to make thyroid hormone. Here's iodide, a large negative ion.

segments.name: Thiocyanate
segments.text: Thiocyanate is a small negative ion about the same size, so it competes with iodide for the pump that pulls iodide into the thyroid.

segments.name: Goitrin
segments.text: Goitrin forms from a glucosinolate in cabbage-family vegetables when they're cut or chewed. Its C=S group interferes with the enzyme that attaches iodine to make the hormone.

segments.name: Goiter
segments.text: With too little iodine and too much of these, the thyroid enlarges to compensate. That's a goiter, which is where the name goitrogen comes from.

segments.name: Who Should Care
segments.text: It's a real problem mainly where iodine is low and a goitrogenic food is a staple, notably cassava. Normal servings of cooked broccoli, kale or cabbage aren't a concern if you get enough iodine.

figures.title: Soaking, Sprouting, Fermenting, Cooking
figures.subtitle: The kitchen fixes, and which foods to pair.

segments.name: Soaking and Sprouting
segments.text: Soaking draws out water-soluble compounds and wakes up the seed's own phytase; pour the water away. Sprouting goes further: the seed breaks down its phytate store to feed the shoot.

segments.name: Fermenting
segments.text: Fermenting lets microbes break compounds down. Sourdough bread, with its long fermentation, has much less phytate than ordinary yeast bread.

segments.name: Boiling and Milling
segments.text: Boiling unfolds proteins like lectins and trypsin inhibitors, and leaches soluble compounds into water you throw away. Milling and peeling remove antinutrients in the bran or skin, but take fiber, vitamins and minerals with them.

segments.name: Pairing Foods
segments.text: Pairing helps too. Vitamin C with plant iron counteracts phytate and tannins. Calcium with high-oxalate foods binds the oxalate. And tea and coffee are best between meals.

segments.name: Heat-Stable or Not
segments.text: Lectins and trypsin inhibitors are proteins, so thorough cooking destroys most of them. Phytate, oxalate and tannins are small, sturdy molecules that survive heat; they're reduced mainly by soaking, sprouting, fermenting, or boiling and draining.

figures.title: Where antinutrients act in the body
figures.subtitle: Tap a number on the cell to see what that part does; the list below it gives every other place in the body.

segments.name: Where Antinutrients Act
segments.text: Here's where antinutrients act: first inside a single cell, then everywhere else in the body. Most work inside the gut, on the minerals and protein in the meal you eat them with. A few are absorbed and reach the kidneys or the thyroid.
segments.cue: The cell drawing and the list of places

segments.name: Inside a Cell
segments.text: Antinutrients mostly work before nutrients reach your cells. Phytates and oxalates bind minerals in the gut, and trypsin inhibitors block protein digestion. A few reach the cell itself: raw bean lectins stick to the sugars on gut cells, and cyanide from unprocessed cassava blocks the mitochondria. Cooking, soaking and fermenting deal with most of them.

foodBody.name: Phytate
foodBody.text: In whole grains, beans and nuts; soaking, sprouting and fermenting reduce it.

foodBody.name: Lectins
foodBody.text: In raw beans and grains; proper cooking makes beans safe.

foodBody.name: Trypsin inhibitors
foodBody.text: In raw soy and legumes; they block a protein-digesting enzyme in the gut and are destroyed by heat.

segments.name: In the Gut
segments.text: In the small intestine, phytate, oxalate and tannins bind iron, zinc and calcium, so less is absorbed. Raw lectins resist digestion and can upset the gut, and trypsin inhibitors block the protein-digesting enzyme the pancreas sends in. Bacteria in the large intestine break down some of what's left.
segments.cue: In the list: small intestine, stomach, pancreas and large intestine

foodBody.name: Phytate
foodBody.text: In whole grains, beans, nuts and seeds. It binds iron and zinc in the gut; soaking, sprouting and fermenting break much of it down.

foodBody.name: Trypsin inhibitors
foodBody.text: In raw soybeans and other beans. They block trypsin, a protein-digesting enzyme; cooking destroys most of them.

segments.name: Beyond the Gut
segments.text: A little oxalate is absorbed and leaves in urine, where it can join calcium to form kidney stones. Goitrogens from raw cabbage-family vegetables and cassava can reduce how much iodine the thyroid takes up, mainly when iodine is already low.
segments.cue: In the list: kidneys and thyroid

foodBody.name: Oxalate
foodBody.text: In spinach, rhubarb, beet greens, nuts and tea. Most stays in the gut bound to calcium; the absorbed part leaves in urine.

segments.name: Simplified
segments.text: This is simplified. In a varied diet, and after soaking or cooking, these effects are small, and many of these compounds have benefits too.

figures.title: Putting It All Together
figures.subtitle: The whole lesson in one table, plus a few extras.

segments.name: One Table
segments.text: Here's the whole lesson in one table: each antinutrient, what it is, what it blocks, where it's found, and the best fix.

segments.name: Worth Knowing
segments.text: A few extras. The same compound can be an antinutrient or a helpful bioactive, depending on the amount, the rest of the diet and how the food is prepared. Cassava, bitter almonds and apricot kernels release cyanide unless they're properly prepared. And green potatoes make solanine, which cooking doesn't destroy, so cut away green parts and sprouts.
